name: Washing clothes properly

lead: Washing clothes properly keeps garments free of odour, dirt and stains so your overall presentation reads as clean. Fresh-smelling, well-kept fabric is noticeable immediately.

Detergent surfactants lift dirt, agitation loosens it and rinsing removes it. Warmer water increases chemical activity and stain solubility. The general laundry reference used does not address odour specifically.

paras: People wash with detergent, agitation and a thorough rinse, then dry fully. Many follow garment care labels, wash gym and worn clothes promptly and avoid leaving damp clothes sitting.
Wikipedia notes heat and agitation can shrink wool and hot water can cause colour loss, so care labels matter.

chain: Odour and residue removed from fabric
Clothes smell fresh on the body
angle.text: Users launder clothes carefully so garments do not hold odour, dirt or stains, which keeps their overall presentation clean. Fresh-smelling, well-kept fabric is an immediately noticeable part of grooming.

lead: Washing clothes properly is a grooming habit that keeps garments clean, fresh-smelling and in good shape, so that a person's outfit looks sharp and does not carry the smell of sweat. In appearance communities it is raised mainly as part of presenting well: clean, intact, correctly fitting clothes with good colour are part of how someone is perceived.[1][2]

Laundry typically involves washing with detergent, agitation, rinsing and drying. Surfactants in modern detergents lift dirt from between fibres, agitation loosens it, and rinsing carries it out.[1] Wikipedia notes that hot water removes dirt more effectively than cold because heat raises the solubility of stains and the activity of cleaning chemicals, while cotton is washed cooler to avoid shrinkage and cold water reduces colour bleeding.[1]

Body odour is produced mostly by skin bacteria breaking down sweat compounds into smaller volatile molecules, with the armpits' apocrine glands as the main source.[2] Management advice in general references centres on bathing, deodorants and antiperspirants.[2]
infobox: Hotter cleans more; cotton cooler to limit shrinkage[1]

paras: Early laundry used running water to carry away dirt and smell, with agitation by rubbing or beating cloth. Modern machines use synthetic powder or liquid detergent, while traditional cleaners included soaproot, yucca and lye-based soap.[1] Dirt trapped deep in fibres is removed in the rinse through a process called diffusiophoresis, described by physicists in 2018.[1]

Many guides advise washing whites separately from coloured items to prevent dye bleeding, and washing similar colours together in cold water reduces bleeding.[1] Care labels use laundry symbols to help consumers avoid problems such as shrinkage and colour bleeding.[1]

Higher temperatures also kill micro-organisms on fabric, although Wikipedia marks that claim as needing a citation.[1] Wool shrinks when heat and agitation cause its fibre scales to stick together, and cotton shrinks slightly when heated, less so if pre-shrunk.[1]
Drying items at 60 degrees Celsius or above for 30 minutes kills dust mites, bed bugs and scabies mites and their eggs, and three hours of direct sunlight kills the eggs.[1]

Bacteria acting on secretions from apocrine sweat glands produce the compounds behind body odour; for example Corynebacterium produces enzymes that split sweat lipids into compounds such as butyric acid.[2] General references recommend daily bathing, deodorants and antiperspirants and note that diet, genetics and health also influence odour.[2] General encyclopedic sources do not address how fabrics retain odour.

timeline.event: Physicists describe diffusiophoresis as a mechanism that removes trapped dirt during rinsing.[1]
